aggregate.basis: TypeScript-only absolute count against the fixed 9-category checklist ceiling; this is a single-language shard. Cross-language common-basis recomputation (restricting to probes where all 10 languages have a fragment) is the responsibility of the aggregation/runner step per interaction_with_quality_metrics.common_basis_rule, and may shift both the denominator (41) and the sum if other languages are NONE on additional probes shared with TypeScript's 3 NONEs, or FULL/PARTIAL where TypeScript is NONE.

metric.hidden_semantic_cost.counting_rule: For each of the 44 frozen probes, the TypeScript measured_fragment (per R5/R6, built under the frozen recipe) was inspected against the 9-category checklist; each category triggered by a genuinely hidden (not locally signaled) behavior is counted once per probe (no double counting of one underlying rule across categories). Probes for which TypeScript has NO documented capability (support level NONE) contribute no fragment and are excluded from the sum and from the denominator, per the interaction_with_quality_metrics common-basis rule (a NONE probe is not scored by A-D; it lowers Capability Coverage C only).
metric.hidden_semantic_cost.methodology_basis: Section D (Hidden Semantic Cost, 20% of quality score) using the frozen 9-category checklist: (a) implicit conversions, (b) hidden writable aliasing/mutation, (c) overload/dynamic dispatch not locally evident, (d) implicit allocation/copy/move/destruction/cleanup, (e) implicit exception/failure propagation, (f) hidden nullability/optionality, (g) implicit representation change, (h) context-dependent overflow/numeric behavior, (i) hidden side effects on existing state. A behavior is NOT counted where the fixed local syntax makes it unambiguous under the TypeScript/JavaScript specification and the frozen recipe (--strict, es2022, nodenext).

per_probe_hidden_cost_counts.note: `const n = 7; return n;` — `number` always denotes IEEE-754 float64; the fragment gives no local signal distinguishing int/float representation (g).
`let counter: number = 0; const LIMIT: number = 100;` — same float64-vs-declared-width representation gap (g); mutability itself is locally evident via let/const.
Definite-assignment analysis makes initialization state locally checked by tsc; only the float64 representation gap remains hidden (g).

TS/JS has no genuinely uninitialized buffer; substituted zero-filled `Uint8Array(16)` (PARTIAL under R9). Allocation/zero-fill is implicit (d); the typed-array's fixed-width integer representation vs `number`'s float64 default is an implicit representation boundary (g).
`x += 1;` on a variable documented as 32-bit but stored as float64: silent loss of exactness above 2^53 rather than int overflow (h); the declared width is not the runtime representation (g).
`xs[1] = 42;` is an explicit, locally-signaled in-place index write; no additional hidden category triggered beyond the intended mutation.
No enforced read-only view exists; the nearest standard form is exposing the same array reference (or a mutable subarray), so writability through `window` is not blocked or signaled (b).
Routing `first` through a one-element array to derive `second` performs an implicit array allocation not visible at the identity-test site (d).

Bare call `f(x)` on an array: JS/TS arrays are always reference-passed, so callee mutation-of-elements capability is invisible at the call site (b); the absence of any copy is itself an implicit, unsignaled allocation/copy decision (d).

No native inout; the required workaround (object/array wrapper) makes the writable-alias mechanism explicit at both declaration and call site, so no additional hidden category is triggered beyond the P-a substitution already recorded elsewhere.
Declaring the closure `neg` performs an implicit heap allocation of a closure object capturing `k`, not signaled at the declaration syntax (d).
Numbers are copied by value on extraction/return; no aliasing or hidden allocation is introduced.
`const [q, r] = [Math.trunc(a/b), a % b];` allocates an implicit tuple array purely as a returning/destructuring vehicle (d).
`a*b+c` on float64-backed values nominally typed as 32-bit integers: silent precision loss beyond 2^53 (h) and representation mismatch between declared width and runtime float64 (g).

`Math.trunc(a/b)`, `a % b` (JS remainder, not floored modulo), and `a/b` for float division: JS `%`'s negative-operand sign behavior is a context-dependent rule (h); the float64 substrate for what is nominally an integer division/remainder is an implicit representation issue (g).
The idiomatic checked-then-wrap form uses `(m + 1) | 0` to force 32-bit wraparound; the bitwise-OR-with-zero idiom is a well-known but non-obvious context-dependent numeric coercion (h).

Plain `a / b` with `b === 0` does not throw; it silently yields `Infinity`/`-Infinity`/`NaN` — failure is never surfaced as an exception or optional value unless an explicit guard is added (e), and this is a context-dependent numeric edge case that differs from most languages' integer division (h).
`s1 === s2` on primitive strings is a documented content comparison in JS/TS; no identity ambiguity or dynamic dispatch is introduced.

`xs.sort((a,b)=>b-a)` mutates `xs` in place and returns the same reference; the in-place aliasing effect on the original array is not signaled by the call form (b), and it is a side effect on existing state beyond the local binding (i).

Simulated narrowing via `big | 0` (bitwise int32 coercion): the actual narrowing rule (two's-complement wraparound of the low 32 bits) is an implicit representation change (g) and a context-dependent numeric behavior not obvious from the syntax (h).

`i + d` between a `number` meant to be integer and a `number` meant to be float: JS performs no visible conversion because both are already float64 — the conversion is total and invisible (a), and the fact that 'int' vs 'float' is purely conventional, not a real representation distinction, is itself hidden (g).

`xs[i]` for out-of-range `i` returns `undefined` rather than throwing or returning a checked optional; under the frozen `--strict` recipe (without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`) the static type of the read is still the element type, not `T | undefined`, so the possible-absence is invisible to the type checker (f) and no exception signals the failure (e).
`xs.slice(1,4)` on a standard Array performs an implicit shallow copy; nothing at the call site signals that this is a copy rather than a shared view (d).
`o ?? 0` (nullish coalescing) precisely targets `null`/`undefined` rather than JS-falsy values, so no additional hidden category beyond the declared optional type.
No standard Option/Maybe chaining operator exists in TS for a bare `number | undefined`; the substituted explicit conditional makes the short-circuit behavior locally visible.

`Number(s)`/`parseInt` do not throw on malformed input; they return `NaN`, a sentinel silently propagated through subsequent arithmetic — failure is never surfaced as an exception at the declared interface (e), and the declared return type (`number`) hides that the value may be the NaN sentinel (f).
Explicit `Number.isNaN(n)` handling is required precisely because the parse's failure mode is an untyped sentinel rather than a checked/exception channel (e).

The discriminant-tagged union and its construction are locally evident from the declared literal-tag type; no additional hidden category beyond family-level structural-typing looseness, which is out of scope for this probe's measured fragment.
`switch` on the tag with an exhaustiveness check (`never`-typed default) makes coverage a compile-time, locally-checked property in the measured fragment as written.

Calling `area()` through the abstract interface dispatches to whichever concrete implementation (`Circle`/`Rect`/`Tri`) is actually referenced; the call site itself gives no local indication of which implementation runs (c).

Generic type parameter `T` is fully erased at runtime; the generic's compile-time type relationship has no runtime representation, which is an implicit representation gap between source and execution (g).
Same type-erasure gap applies to the constrained generic `max_of<T>`; the interface constraint enforced at compile time vanishes at runtime (g).
`item.tag()` on a `Named[]` dispatches to `A` or `B`'s implementation without local evidence of which (c); the heterogeneous array's element type is erased at runtime (g).
`xs.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0)` allocates an implicit closure for the reducer not visible as an allocation site (d).

`mp.get('b') ?? 0` — `Map.get` on a missing key returns `undefined`, a hidden nullability not reflected without the explicit fallback (f); iteration order is in fact guaranteed by spec (insertion order), so no cost is charged there.

`fs.promises.readFile`/`fs.open` calls that can reject/throw are wrapped in `try/finally`; the possible-failure channel (Promise rejection or thrown error) is implicit at the call unless the signature is inspected (e).

TypeScript under the frozen `es2022` target has no deterministic destructor and no `using`/explicit-resource-management syntax (that feature targets ES2023+); the substituted explicit close-call-at-scope-end form makes the cleanup point fully visible in the fragment as written.
`console.log("x")` requires no import; the side effect is the entire declared purpose of the statement, not a hidden one.

TypeScript's module-private/exported distinction is a compile-time-only convention; the emitted JavaScript retains no runtime privacy enforcement, so the 'private' guarantee is an implicit representation gap between source and compiled behavior (g).

`Promise.all([...])` reads as 'concurrent' but executes on a single-threaded cooperative event loop; the true execution model is not evident from the async/await syntax (c); an unhandled rejection from either promise propagates implicitly rather than through a locally visible channel unless explicitly caught (e).

Race-freedom here relies on the JS run-to-completion guarantee for synchronous statements within a single event-loop turn; this normative guarantee is documented but not signaled by any construct at the increment site itself (c).

metric.hidden_semantic_cost.status: TypeScript hidden_semantic_cost measured for all 44 frozen probes; 3 scored NONE (no fragment, excluded from A-D per spec) and cited; 41 fragments checklist-scored with itemized per-probe category counts.

typescript_none_probes_excluded.reason: TypeScript/JavaScript has no documented mechanism for a second name to hold a writable reference/pointer to an existing scalar local; primitives are always passed/aliased by value. NONE per canonical_task's own N4 clause.
Node/TypeScript has no built-in FFI mechanism reaching a C function without a third-party native addon (node-ffi) or a separate native build step outside the frozen recipe. NONE per N-2.

Node/TypeScript cannot export a stable unmangled C-ABI symbol from source using only the frozen tsc/node recipe; doing so requires a native addon toolchain (node-gyp/N-API) outside the frozen recipe. NONE per N-1/N-2; no compiled artifact under the frozen recipe for `nm` verification.
